Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher owning two weekly newspapers, filed a class action antitrust suit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet on behalf of news publishers. The suit alleges that Google violates the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust laws by siphoning off publishers' content, readers, and ad revenue through anticompetitive means, thereby starving the free press and causing publishers to lose billions of dollars.

The lawsuit specifically targets Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot, citing them as technologies that worsen the problem for publishers. It also targets Google's Knowledge Graph, launched in May 2012, alleging that much of the 'collective intelligence' within it was misappropriated from publishers. The Knowledge Graph, compiled by extracting information from publishers' websites and open source/licensed databases, contained 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities by 2020. Google's Knowledge Panel displays summaries drawn from this database to the right of search results, and its 'Featured Snippets' technology, which algorithmically extracts answers from webpages, is cited as shifting traffic away from publishers. A Wall Street Journal report noted that when The Atlantic modeled Google integrating AI into search, 75% of the time AI would answer queries without a click-through to the publisher's site.

Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating that Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, with news sites being the third-largest category of AI training data. The case alleges changing AdSense rates and improper spoliation of evidence via Google's destruction of chat messages, an issue raised in the recent Epic Games antitrust lawsuit which Epic won. The suit seeks damages and an injunction requiring Google to obtain publisher consent to use website data for training general AI products, including Google's own and rivals', and allows publishers opting out of SGE to appear in search results.

The U.S. lawsuit follows a last-month agreement where Google pays Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) annually, distributed by headcount, after Meta began blocking Canadian news in August under new laws. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. Hausfeld law firm states that Google's anticompetitive scheme harms competition, consumers, labor, and a democratic free press. A Google spokesperson called the lawsuit meritless, claiming Google links people to publisher websites more than 24 billion times monthly at no cost.

    hash: e68c1138
---

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states aiming to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

During the trial, Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals with Apple and partners to make Google the default search engine. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. Pichai stated the decision to pay for defaults was made with the consumer in mind, to gather data and be the best search engine across devices. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device to create inseparable services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software. In February, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours; Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed turning off history for a personnel matter unrelated to the hold. In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior; Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case is expected to continue for several weeks, potentially resulting in a Microsoft-like outcome where Google must change behavior, share APIs, and be banned from exclusive deals; Google might have to turn over collected data to other search engines, given the DOJ noted Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, with ripple effects on FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.

Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices. Although the ISA has existed since 2002, Cue negotiated the current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. During renegotiation, Apple sought a higher revenue share, while Pichai wanted to maintain the deal; they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue stated there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and that this remains true today. He argued the deal was driven by factors beyond economics, noting Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choice during setup, reasoning that showing engines users had not heard of would be detrimental. He further stated Apple makes Google the default because it is the best, while acknowledging users can easily change it, contrasting this with DuckDuckGo's CEO testimony that switching takes too many steps.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple prioritizes user privacy and offers better protection than Google, citing ISA provisions requiring login-free searching and Apple's efforts to prevent tracking. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw suggested it might be significant, but Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the agreement succeeds due to the platform's overall appeal. Additionally, Google lawyer John Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, highlighting seamless Google integration as a key user interface innovation mentioned in early promotional materials before 2003. Cue explained that pre-2003 users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple introduced functionality allowing non-URL text in the URL field to trigger searches. Schmidtlein also argued Google helped Safari succeed by being a great product, referencing deals with Yahoo and Bing, and both men claimed switching search engines is easy and a non-issue.

Google Search is frequently favored by users due to its ability to personalize mobile widgets and services through extensive data collection on searches, smart speaker interactions, and ad clicks, a capability Bing lacks. While Bing has recently overhauled its layout with generative AI and offered comparative search results (e.g., for 'kids BMX bike green'), it has faced criticism for returning options over $300 when asked for those under $200, whereas DuckDuckGo ignored the color specification in the query. Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, argues that Google is the preferred choice of users, browsers, and device makers because it is the best in business, noting that switching providers is easy and users often revert to Google as default. He claims the industry is competitive and that users choose Google voluntarily rather than being forced. Despite Google's market share advantages stemming from its scale, longevity, and user data, proving it broke the law to maintain this status quo in the US is described as an uphill battle. Controversies include allegations that Google manipulates search results to maximize ad revenue, a claim admitted by former DuckDuckGo VP Megan Grey (though she may have misinterpreted evidence) and supported by a Wired article that was later removed for not meeting standards. Google's official response, provided by Danny Sullivan, distinguishes between long-standing ad keyword matching and separate organic result matching systems that handle meaning and spelling. Additionally, search quality is argued to have improved since 2013 due to a massive increase in data volume from 9 ZB to 120 ZB, driven by live information in apps rather than static websites.

Sam Altman is a backer of Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time. At its annual hardware event, Google announced updates to the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro notes it is similar to the Pixel 7 Pro but offers improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI features, though it has an underutilized temperature sensor. Dave Clark, ousted as Flexport CEO just a year into his job, criticized the company's founder and board following CNBC reporting on his departure; Flexport is valued at $8 billion. A book by Michael Lewis, 'Going Infinite,' debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's Manhattan Federal Court trial, revealing details about SBF's attempt to buy off Trump to prevent him from running for president again. Prosecutors in the SBF trial accused Bankman-Fried of knowingly committing fraud for wealth and power, while the defense argued he acted in good faith and got over his head. LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool. Elon Musk claimed X generated 100–200 million daily posts in September, while CEO Linda Yaccarino later stated the figure was 500 million posts per day. IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, laid off staff after failing to gain traction post-IPO in August 2021 despite raising over $400 million. Esther Rodriguez-Villegas from Acurable, a medical device company making wearables for sleep apnea and epilepsy, explains existing devices make detecting and treating these conditions difficult. Breathe Battery Technologies created software that can be added to lithium-ion batteries to enable faster charging or greater longevity. A survey of 10 investors highlighted where startups can succeed, the impact of oligopoly dynamics, and the value of proprietary data in the future of AI. Gmail announced stricter rules for bulk senders starting next year.

Question: Which company, recently discussed in TechCrunch articles for both hosting an annual hardware event to showcase new developments and being the subject of a class action antitrust lawsuit by news publishers for its alleged anticompetitive practices, is also known for its search engine and advertising services?

### tech-news/helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md

Title: Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google over AI harms

Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher owning two weekly newspapers, filed a class action antitrust suit in the U.S. District Court in D.C. against Google and Alphabet on behalf of news publishers. The suit alleges that Google violates the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust laws by siphoning off publishers' content, readers, and ad revenue through anticompetitive means, thereby starving the free press and causing publishers to lose billions of dollars.

The lawsuit specifically targets Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot, citing them as technologies that worsen the problem for publishers. It also targets Google's Knowledge Graph, launched in May 2012, alleging that much of the 'collective intelligence' within it was misappropriated from publishers. The Knowledge Graph, compiled by extracting information from publishers' websites and open source/licensed databases, contained 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities by 2020. Plus cites a 2023 News Media Alliance report and a Washington Post article stating that Google's Bard AI was trained on news, magazine, and digital publications, with news sites being the third-largest category of AI training data. The case alleges changing AdSense rates and improper spoliation of evidence via Google's destruction of chat messages, an issue raised in the recent Epic Games antitrust lawsuit which Epic won. The case arrives alongside the U.S. Justice Department's lawsuit against Google for monopolizing digital ad technologies, referencing a 2020 DOJ civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising. ### legal-trials/google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-trial-developments.md

Title: Google antitrust case: key facts and trial developments
Summary: Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO testimony, financial data on default search engine deals, and potential regulatory outcomes.

The U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google stems from a 2020 claim regarding its dominance in the online search market, separate from a January filing by the Department of Justice and eight states aiming to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme. The government argues Google uses platforms and deals to block competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing data needed to improve products. Google argues its actions are legal business practices because being the default engine is desirable, not illegal.

During the trial, Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified, defending tactics including deals with Apple and partners to make Google the default search engine. Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on October 28 that Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 to make itself the default search engine across platforms, including attempts to preinstall Chrome on iPhones. About $18 billion of the $26.3 billion total went directly to Apple; Google's deal with Apple has been in place since 2003. Pichai stated the decision to pay for defaults was made with the consumer in mind, to gather data and be the best search engine across devices. A 2007 Google product strategy meeting email showed that when users changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches, dropping 27% when they switched away.

Pichai admitted in 2018 attempting to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device to create inseparable services, hoping for a win-win where Google gains search users/data and Apple gains revenue from a search agreement, but Cook declined as Apple does not preload third-party software. In February, the DOJ accused Google of systematically destroying chats via a history-off option deleting messages every 24 hours; Pichai claimed he took action against the history-off default in February to comply with the DOJ's litigation hold, though Bellshaw cited a 2021 message exchange where Pichai discussed turning off history for a personnel matter unrelated to the hold. In 2005, Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, prompting Google's legal chief David Drummond to send an angry letter accusing this of anticompetitive behavior; Bellshaw used Drummond's letter to highlight Google's hypocrisy regarding defaults, noting that changes to defaults worsen problems and most users do not change them, arguments also used by DuckDuckGo, Brave, and Bing against Google.

The case is expected to continue for several weeks, potentially resulting in a Microsoft-like outcome where Google must change behavior, share APIs, and be banned from exclusive deals; Google might have to turn over collected data to other search engines, given the DOJ noted Google gets 16 times more data than Bing daily, with ripple effects on FTC cases against Amazon, Apple, and Facebook.

### legal-trials/apple-defends-google-search-deal-in-court-there-wasn-t-a.md

Title: Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'
Summary: Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argued the deal prioritized user experience and privacy over economics.

Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices. Although the ISA has existed since 2002, Cue negotiated the current iteration with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. During renegotiation, Apple sought a higher revenue share, while Pichai wanted to maintain the deal; they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue stated there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and that this remains true today. He argued the deal was driven by factors beyond economics, noting Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choice during setup, reasoning that showing engines users had not heard of would be detrimental. He further stated Apple makes Google the default because it is the best, while acknowledging users can easily change it, contrasting this with DuckDuckGo's CEO testimony that switching takes too many steps.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple prioritizes user privacy and offers better protection than Google, citing ISA provisions requiring login-free searching and Apple's efforts to prevent tracking. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw suggested it might be significant, but Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the agreement succeeds due to the platform's overall appeal. Additionally, Google lawyer John Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, highlighting seamless Google integration as a key user interface innovation mentioned in early promotional materials before 2003. Cue explained that pre-2003 users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple introduced functionality allowing non-URL text in the URL field to trigger searches. Schmidtlein also argued Google helped Safari succeed by being a great product, referencing deals with Yahoo and Bing, and both men claimed switching search engines is easy and a non-issue.

### tech-news/google-search-vs-competitors-data-manipulation-and-market.md

Title: Google Search vs Competitors: Data, Manipulation, and Market Dominance
Summary: An analysis of Google's data-driven personalization, user preference arguments, and controversies regarding search result manipulation versus competitor performance.

Google Search is frequently favored by users due to its ability to personalize mobile widgets and services through extensive data collection on searches, smart speaker interactions, and ad clicks, a capability Bing lacks. While Bing has recently overhauled its layout with generative AI and offered comparative search results (e.g., for 'kids BMX bike green'), it has faced criticism for returning options over $300 when asked for those under $200, whereas DuckDuckGo ignored the color specification in the query. Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, argues that Google is the preferred choice of users, browsers, and device makers because it is the best in business, noting that switching providers is easy and users often revert to Google as default. He claims the industry is competitive and that users choose Google voluntarily rather than being forced. Despite Google's market share advantages stemming from its scale, longevity, and user data, proving it broke the law to maintain this status quo in the US is described as an uphill battle. Controversies include allegations that Google manipulates search results to maximize ad revenue, a claim admitted by former DuckDuckGo VP Megan Grey (though she may have misinterpreted evidence) and supported by a Wired article that was later removed for not meeting standards. Google's official response, provided by Danny Sullivan, distinguishes between long-standing ad keyword matching and separate organic result matching systems that handle meaning and spelling. Additionally, search quality is argued to have improved since 2013 due to a massive increase in data volume from 9 ZB to 120 ZB, driven by live information in apps rather than static websites.

### tech-news/tech-news-sam-altman-backs-teen-startup-google-unveils-pixel.md

Title: Tech News: Sam Altman backs teen startup, Google unveils Pixel 8, and more industry updates
Summary: Sam Altman supports a teen-founded AI startup; Google launches the Pixel 8 series and Android 14; LinkedIn adds AI tools; and various startups and executives face challenges or new developments.

Sam Altman is a backer of Induced AI, a startup founded this year by two teenagers that automates business workflows by converting plain English instructions to pseudo-code in real time. At its annual hardware event, Google announced updates to the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. A review of the Pixel 8 Pro notes it is similar to the Pixel 7 Pro but offers improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI features, though it has an underutilized temperature sensor. Dave Clark, ousted as Flexport CEO just a year into his job, criticized the company's founder and board following CNBC reporting on his departure; Flexport is valued at $8 billion. A book by Michael Lewis, 'Going Infinite,' debuted on the first day of Sam Bankman-Fried's Manhattan Federal Court trial, revealing details about SBF's attempt to buy off Trump to prevent him from running for president again. Prosecutors in the SBF trial accused Bankman-Fried of knowingly committing fraud for wealth and power, while the defense argued he acted in good faith and got over his head. LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool. Elon Musk claimed X generated 100–200 million daily posts in September, while CEO Linda Yaccarino later stated the figure was 500 million posts per day. IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, laid off staff after failing to gain traction post-IPO in August 2021 despite raising over $400 million. Esther Rodriguez-Villegas from Acurable, a medical device company making wearables for sleep apnea and epilepsy, explains existing devices make detecting and treating these conditions difficult. Breathe Battery Technologies created software that can be added to lithium-ion batteries to enable faster charging or greater longevity. A survey of 10 investors highlighted where startups can succeed, the impact of oligopoly dynamics, and the value of proprietary data in the future of AI. Gmail announced stricter rules for bulk senders starting next year.
